definition.text: An economy or market is efficient when it gets the most of what people want, such as well-being, out of the resources it has; economists usually mean allocative (Pareto) or productive efficiency.

facts.text: Allocative or Pareto efficiency means no change could help one person without harming another; productive efficiency means no more of one good can be made without making less of another, at the lowest average cost.
The two ideas are not the same: a market can be allocatively efficient without being productively efficient, or the other way round.
Because productive resources are scarce, they must go to each industry in just the right amounts, or too much or too little gets produced.
One school of thought stresses the distortions that governments create; another stresses the distortions that markets create and wants more government involvement to fix them.
The first welfare theorem says a perfectly competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient, but this only holds without market imperfections, which are significant in real markets.
Efficiency in the Pareto sense says nothing about equality or the overall well-being of a society.
Removing one market distortion does not always raise efficiency: if another distortion cannot be removed, the theory of the second best says efficiency may even fall.
Many economists consider carbon pricing the most economically efficient way to cut greenhouse gas emissions.

definition.text: The branch of economics that uses the tools of microeconomics to judge how well off a society is as a whole.

facts.text: Welfare economics guides public economics, which studies how government action can improve social welfare, and it is the theoretical basis of cost–benefit analysis.
Its first fundamental theorem says competitive markets, under certain assumptions, give Pareto efficient outcomes, an idea sometimes linked to Adam Smith's invisible hand.
Its second theorem says any Pareto efficient outcome can be reached through a competitive market if a planner first makes lump-sum transfers.
Arrow's impossibility theorem is sometimes counted as a third fundamental theorem of welfare economics.
The early neoclassical approach was built by Edgeworth, Sidgwick, Marshall and Pigou; the later 'new welfare economics' rests on the work of Pareto, Kaldor, Hicks and Scitovsky.
The idea of an externality, developed by Pigou, remains central to modern welfare economics and to environmental economics.
Amartya Sen urged welfare research to use a wider range of data and to discuss ethics and morality openly.
Austrian school economists reject both cardinal and ordinal welfare economics because they rely on comparing different people's utility.

definition.text: A rule that ranks possible states of society from more to less desirable by combining the preferences of everyone in it.

facts.text: Economists use social welfare functions to decide which of two outcomes, such as two income distributions, is better for society as a whole.
Unlike one consumer's utility function, it maps many people's utility functions onto a single result.
Ordinal versions use only whether one option is better than another; cardinal versions also use how much better it is.
Abram Bergson introduced the term in a 1938 article to state precisely the value judgements needed to define maximum economic welfare.
In 1935 Lionel Robbins argued that changes in different people's utilities cannot be compared by any empirical test.
Arrow's impossibility theorem shows that, unlike a single consumer, a society cannot build a fully consistent decision rule from ranked preferences alone.

definition.text: A social welfare function that takes numerical measures of each person's well-being, often income, and turns them into one number for the whole society's welfare.

facts.text: The utilitarian or Benthamite version adds up individual utilities, so it maximizes total income without caring how that income is shared.
Under the utilitarian version, society should accept a transfer from poor to rich if the rich gain more utility than the poor lose.
The max-min or Rawlsian version, based on John Rawls, judges society by the welfare of its worst-off member alone.
The max-min function can be read as society showing an extreme aversion to uncertainty, caring only about the worst position anyone could face.
In 1973 Amartya Sen proposed a welfare function equal to average income multiplied by one minus the Gini index.

definition.text: The result that if society's choices follow the rules of rational choice under risk, the social welfare function must be the utilitarian sum of individual utilities.

facts.text: By the theorem, any non-utilitarian rule is incoherent: it will accept some bets that every member of society opposes.
With a weaker condition, that rankings do not depend on the unit (cents or dollars), the welfare function must belong to the isoelastic family.
In that family, one parameter value gives the Nash bargaining solution (maximizing the product of utilities) and another gives the utilitarian sum.
Requiring the Pigou–Dalton principle, that inequality is not a good thing, limits the parameter to at most 1.

definition.text: The four marginal conditions on consumption and production that must all hold for an economy to be Pareto efficient.

facts.text: Every consumer must have the same marginal rate of substitution between any two goods, so no swap between consumers can make both happier.
Every producer must have the same marginal rate of transformation between two goods, so shifting production between producers cannot raise total output.
A factor such as labour must have the same marginal product at every producer of a good, so moving production cannot cut its cost.
Consumers' marginal rates of substitution must equal producers' marginal rates of transformation, so changing the product mix cannot make consumers happier.

definition.text: The conditions, such as monopoly, hidden information or poorly designed regulation, that keep an economy from reaching Pareto efficiency.

facts.text: Imperfect market structures such as monopoly, monopsony, oligopoly and monopolistic competition cause inefficiency.
Asymmetric information, including principal–agent problems, and the falling long-run costs of a natural monopoly also cause inefficiency.
Government limits on prices and quantities and other regulation arising from government failure can also make an economy inefficient.
One inefficiency can offset another: if pollution leads to too many tyres being made, a tax on tyres might restore the efficient amount.

definition.text: The conflict that arises because policies making the economy fairer usually cost some efficiency, so society must choose between the two.

facts.text: Redistributing income is costly, so there is a built-in choice between more efficiency and more equity.
Much economic research therefore measures the efficiency losses of tax and transfer programmes, which redistribute by their nature.
The trade-off is at the heart of many debates about tax policy; its formal study was begun by James Mirrlees in 1971.
Because real markets are imperfect, emissions trading may also involve a trade-off between equity and efficiency.

definition.text: The early neoclassical approach to welfare, built by Edgeworth, Sidgwick, Marshall and Pigou, which treated utility as measurable and added it up across people.

facts.text: It assumed utility can be measured on a scale, that preferences are fixed and stable, and that each extra unit consumed adds less and less utility.
With those assumptions a social welfare function is simply the sum of all individual utility functions, in the tradition of Bentham.
It was often inferred that moving income from a rich person to a poor person tends to raise total utility.

definition.text: The ordinal approach to welfare, based on the work of Pareto, Kaldor, Hicks and Scitovsky, which judges efficiency without measuring or comparing people's utility.

facts.text: It treats efficiency and distribution separately: efficiency is judged by Pareto and Kaldor–Hicks criteria, distribution by the choice of social welfare function.
It replaces measurable utility with ordinal utility, which only ranks bundles of goods, for example on an indifference-curve map.
The consensus behind it largely collapsed after Arrow's impossibility theorem and utility representation theorems showed such approaches to be self-contradictory.
Murray Rothbard proposed rebuilding welfare economics on 'demonstrated preference', under which only voluntary market exchanges clearly raise welfare.

definition.text: A situation is Pareto efficient when there is no longer any way to make one person better off without making someone else worse off.

facts.text: A Pareto improvement is a change that leaves at least one person better off and nobody worse off; Pareto efficiency is reached once no such change is left.
Example: if Smith owns an apple but wants an orange, and Jones owns an orange but wants an apple, the situation is inefficient because trading makes both better off.
It is named after Vilfredo Pareto (1848–1923), an Italian engineer and economist who used it to study economic efficiency and income distribution.
Pareto called it 'optimal', but it does not pick one best outcome; it only marks out a set of outcomes, which is why 'efficiency' fits better.
Pareto efficiency does not mean fairness: an economy where a wealthy few hold most resources can still be Pareto efficient.
Market failure is a case where markets do not produce an efficient allocation, so a Pareto improvement is possible.
In social choice theory the same idea is called the unanimity principle: if everyone prefers A to B, society should too.

Because asymmetric information, adverse selection and moral hazard make Pareto efficiency hard to judge in practice, most people do not take the welfare theorems as accurate descriptions of the real world.

definition.text: A situation is weakly Pareto efficient if no change could make every single person strictly better off.

facts.text: A strong Pareto improvement makes all agents strictly better off, while an ordinary Pareto improvement needs only one strictly better off and the rest no worse.
Every strong Pareto improvement is also a weak one, but not the reverse, so a weakly efficient outcome may not be fully Pareto efficient.

definition.text: A weaker form of Pareto efficiency that recognises a planner such as a government may be unable to improve on an inefficient market outcome because it faces the same limits as everyone else.

facts.text: It matters when people hold private information, such as a worker's own productivity or a used car's quality, leading to moral hazard or adverse selection.
A planner usually has no more information than market participants, so it can only use anonymous rules or rules based on observable behaviour.
If no allowed rule can improve on the market outcome, that outcome is called constrained Pareto optimal.

definition.text: The link showing that maximizing a weighted sum of everyone's utility, with positive weights, always gives a Pareto efficient allocation, and under some assumptions every efficient allocation can be found that way.

facts.text: An allocation that maximizes a positively weighted sum of utilities must be Pareto efficient, since any Pareto improvement would raise the sum.
Takashi Negishi proved that, under certain assumptions, every Pareto efficient allocation maximizes such a weighted sum for some set of positive weights.

title: Kaldor–Hicks efficiency

definition.text: A change counts as a Kaldor–Hicks improvement if the people who gain could, in principle, fully compensate the people who lose, even if they never actually do.

facts.text: It is a looser test than a Pareto improvement, useful because almost any real policy change makes at least one person worse off.
Every Pareto improvement is a Kaldor–Hicks improvement, but most Kaldor–Hicks improvements are not Pareto improvements.
Example: a deal that causes pollution is a Kaldor–Hicks improvement if buyers and sellers would still go ahead while fully compensating the pollution's victims.
The Kaldor test asks whether gainers would pay enough to win losers' consent; the Hicks test asks whether losers could not afford to bribe gainers to drop the change.
It is named after the twentieth-century economists Nicholas Kaldor and John Hicks.
It underpins cost–benefit analysis: approving a project when benefits exceed costs is the same as requiring that winners could compensate losers.
Critics ask why the mere ability to compensate losers should matter morally if compensation is never paid, and note that it ignores income distribution.
The Kaldor–Hicks compensation principle is the standard criterion in cost–benefit analysis of climate change.

contested_note: Critics dispute why hypothetical compensation that is never paid should carry moral weight in deciding policy.

title: Distributive justice

definition.text: The question of how a society's resources, goods and opportunities should be shared out fairly among its members.

facts.text: Distributive justice looks at outcomes, in contrast with fair process and formal equal opportunity.
Most modern theories of distributive justice start from the fact that material resources are scarce.
Leading theories include Rawls's justice as fairness, utilitarianism, egalitarianism and Marxism's 'from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs'.
In an environmental setting it means sharing a society's environmental risks, harms and benefits fairly; such burdens fall mostly on the Global South while benefits go mainly to the Global North.
In climate justice, distributive justice asks who bears the costs of climate change and of the actions taken against it.
Friedrich von Hayek called distributive justice meaningless in a market system, where outcomes arise spontaneously rather than by anyone's design.
Robert Nozick argued in Anarchy, State, and Utopia that the term is not neutral, because no central distributor hands out shares.

contested_note: Theorists hold widely different conceptions of distributive justice, and libertarians such as Hayek and Nozick reject the idea itself.

definition.text: The different rules a group can use to share out rewards and costs, such as equal shares, shares by contribution, or shares by need.

facts.text: Donelson R. Forsyth defines five norms: equality, equity, power, need and responsibility.
Under equality everyone gets the same share whatever they put in; under equity people who contribute more receive more.
Members of large groups prefer to share rewards and costs according to equity.
Under the need norm, those in greatest need get more resources regardless of what they contributed.

definition.text: John Rawls's theory, set out in A Theory of Justice, that a just society gives equal rights and liberties, equal opportunity, and arranges inequalities to benefit the least advantaged.

facts.text: Rawls roots justice in society's 'basic structure', the fundamental rules that shape its institutions and so its citizens' life chances.
The first principle, the liberty principle, gives everyone equal access to basic rights and liberties.
The second principle, the difference principle, allows inequalities only if they bring the greatest benefit to the least advantaged and positions stay open to all.

definition.text: The view, based on the equal worth of all people, that citizens should be treated equally in respect and concern by the state and by one another.

facts.text: Egalitarianism focuses on unchosen circumstances that hold people back, and its central problem is deciding which kind of equality to pursue.
Strict egalitarianism insists on equal shares even when an unequal split would make everyone better off, so it can produce Pareto-inefficient outcomes.
Equality of welfare concerns outcomes; critics favour equality of prospects instead, such as equality of opportunity.

definition.text: A situation where a competitive market for some good would make everyone better off, yet no such market exists.

facts.text: Pollution is the classic case: a factory dumping waste into a river harms people downstream, but has no incentive to count that harm, so no market for pollution forms.
Markets can also be missing because of coordination failures such as the free-rider problem, difficulty monitoring who causes harm, high transaction costs, or lack of trust and information.
Alternative fuels show the chicken-and-egg problem: stations won't sell a fuel until such cars exist, and people won't buy the cars until stations exist.
Governments can create the missing conditions; for pollution, a popular solution is assigning property rights so the parties can bargain, as in the Coase theorem.
Economists may try to avoid waste by creating missing markets so that efficient trading can happen where none existed before.

definition.text: A state of the economy in which the mix of goods produced matches what people want, so that society's welfare is as high as it can be.

facts.text: It is reached when each good's marginal benefit to consumers is at least the marginal cost of producing it; for a firm in a perfect market this means price equals marginal cost.
With no externalities, the market equilibrium is where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost, so net social benefit is maximized.
At that point social surplus is maximized and there is no deadweight loss.
Example: at an output of 40 the marginal cost is $6 but buyers would pay $15, so the good is under-consumed; the efficient output is 70, where marginal cost equals marginal utility.
A monopoly can set price above marginal cost, making the allocation inefficient and causing a deadweight welfare loss.
When a market fails to allocate resources efficiently, through imperfect knowledge, market power or externalities, there is market failure.
Pareto efficiency is possible without allocative efficiency, when no one can gain without someone losing but gainers could gain more than losers lose.

definition.text: Kenneth Arrow's proof that no way of combining people's rankings of options into a group ranking can meet all the basic requirements of rational choice.

facts.text: In particular, no such rule can satisfy independence of irrelevant alternatives, so in voting no ranked system can fully avoid the spoiler effect.
Arrow proved the theorem in 1950, founding modern social choice theory, a branch of welfare economics that studies how to combine preferences across a society.
It generalizes Condorcet's voting paradox: with three voters and three options, the majority can prefer A to B, B to C and C to A even though each voter is consistent.
Arrow remarked that most voting systems do not work badly all the time; he only proved that all can work badly at times.
Black's median voter theorem showed that if voters and candidates lie along a single left-right spectrum, Arrow's conditions can all be met by majority rule.
The theorem depends on people giving rankings; rated voting systems that ask for scores, such as 0–10, can escape it.
By the 1950s some economists claimed the theorem proved that any attempt to build normative standards in economics was doomed.

definition.text: The principle that a choice between two options, A and B, should not depend on how anyone feels about some third, unrelated option C.

facts.text: For a voting rule, it means society's ranking of A against B should not flip just because voters change their view of A against C.
It is equivalent to saying an election should be free of spoiler candidates.
Behavioural economists have found that individuals themselves violate it, for example through decoy effects.

definition.text: A measure of income inequality, developed by the British economist Anthony Atkinson, that lets the user choose how much to care about inequality.

facts.text: Its parameter ε, the 'inequality aversion' level, makes the index more sensitive to the bottom of the income distribution as it rises.
The index gives the share of current income that could be given up, without lowering social welfare, if incomes were made perfectly equal.
It runs from 0 to 1 and is zero only when all incomes are the same; with ε = 0 (no aversion to inequality) it is always zero.
It is tied to a generalized entropy index, so overall inequality can be broken down by groups, which the Gini index cannot do.

definition.text: A way of judging human welfare by what people are actually able to do and be in leading lives they value, not just by their rights or income.

facts.text: Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum developed it in the 1980s as an alternative to traditional welfare economics.
'Functionings' are the beings and doings that make up a life, such as being healthy or safe; 'capabilities' are the combinations of functionings a person can really achieve.
Sen argues that utility-based welfare economics ignores how welfare is distributed, neglects rights and freedoms, and is misled by people adapting to bad conditions.
Resource- or income-based measures struggle because people differ in their ability to turn resources into valuable activities.
Nussbaum lists 10 central capabilities and holds that a decent political order must secure at least a threshold level of each for everyone.
The approach led to the UN's Human Development Index, first published in 1990, which equally weighted health, education and income.
It looks at the capabilities people enjoy within a country rather than total GDP, and is closely linked to sustainability within a generation.

title: Compensation principle

definition.text: A rule in welfare economics that favours a change if those who gain from it could compensate those who lose and still leave nobody worse off.

facts.text: The Pareto criterion is a strict form in which compensation must actually happen, not just be possible.
The principle is controversial when full compensation is possible but not paid, leaving some people as losers.
Many neoclassical economists judge an intervention good if total gains exceed total losses, even if losers are not compensated in practice.
In cost–benefit analysis of climate policy, a project that benefits some, compensates losers and still leaves something over is an unambiguous welfare gain.

contested_note: Its use is disputed where compensation is feasible but not actually paid.

definition.text: The set of final splits of two goods between two people that they could reach by trading to mutual benefit from their starting holdings; every point on it is Pareto efficient.

facts.text: It is drawn in an Edgeworth box, with each person's holdings measured from opposite corners.
The two people keep trading as long as their marginal rates of substitution differ; on the curve their indifference curves just touch and the rates are equal.
The analysis cannot say where on the curve they end up; that depends on their bargaining skills.
Any Walrasian (competitive) equilibrium lies on the contract curve.

definition.text: The way an economy's total output, income or wealth is shared out among people or among the factors of production such as labour, land and capital.

facts.text: Studies of household income often look at the share going to the top or bottom slices, such as fifths, of households and at what drives those shares.
Distribution has been central to political economy since the 19th century, in the work of Adam Smith, David Ricardo and John Stuart Mill.
Welfare economics separates how much output is possible from how the resulting income is distributed.
In neoclassical theory, supply and demand in factor markets set equilibrium output, income and its distribution.
Vilfredo Pareto proposed that income follows a power law, now called the Pareto distribution.
Ecological economics treats fair distribution as a goal alongside efficient allocation and a sustainable scale of the economy.

definition.text: An economy is dynamically efficient when it invests less than the return to capital, so that no generation can be made better off without making another worse off.

facts.text: In the Solow growth model, saving above the Golden Rule rate is dynamically inefficient: the economy could be better off today and tomorrow by saving less.
In overlapping-generations models people may save more than is socially optimal, causing dynamic inefficiency.
A 1989 study by Abel, Mankiw, Summers and Zeckhauser suggested the United States and other OECD countries are dynamically efficient.
In industrial economics, some argue that business concentration or monopolies can promote dynamic efficiency.

definition.text: A diagram of a tiny market with just two goods and two consumers, where each point in the box is one way of splitting the goods between them.

facts.text: The box's sides equal the total amounts of the two goods; each consumer's holdings are measured from opposite corners, and their indifference curves show what they prefer.
It is named after Francis Ysidro Edgeworth, who presented it in 1881; Pareto turned it into the familiar box in 1906 and Bowley popularized it.
Points where the two consumers' indifference curves touch are Pareto optima; together they form the Pareto set or efficient locus.
Market equilibria are where both indifference curves touch a common price line, so the equilibria are exactly the Pareto optima: the first welfare theorem in pictures.
For the second welfare theorem, a government need not hand out the exact desired allocation; it can shift resources onto the right price line and let the market finish the job.

definition.text: Fairness in economics: the idea of justice in how wealth, resources and taxes are shared within a society.

facts.text: Equity means economic processes and outcomes do not unduly favour or disadvantage any group or person.
Equity is judged separately from economic efficiency when assessing social welfare, and is often measured with tools such as the Gini index.
It is hard to define because it depends on social values and would require comparing different people's utility.
Peter Corning names three kinds of fairness, equality, equity and reciprocity, that must be balanced for a truly fair society.
Experimental economics studies equity as inequity aversion.
For the Kyoto Protocol's flexible mechanisms, economists argued that equity could be separated from efficiency, handled for example through how emission rights are allocated between countries.

definition.text: Two fairness principles for taxes and public services: treat people in similar situations alike (horizontal), and treat people with more ability to pay differently (vertical).

facts.text: Horizontal equity says people with similar incomes should carry similar tax burdens; it links to tax neutrality.
Vertical equity says the better-off should pay more, supporting progressive taxes whose rates rise with income or wealth.
A tax taking the same share from all is proportional; one taking a rising share from the rich is progressive, a main tool for reducing inequality.
Both are hard to apply: defining similar situations is subjective, and vertical equity runs into problems of comparing utility across people.

definition.text: The economic loss a society suffers, beyond the money collected, because taxes or subsidies change how people behave; also called the deadweight loss of taxation.

facts.text: Adam Smith first discussed excess burdens; subsidies, which act as negative taxes, cause the same kind of inefficiency.
Estimates of losses from taxes range from 2.5 cents to 30 cents per dollar of revenue on average, and much higher at the margin.
As a rule of thumb, the excess burden of a tax rises with the square of the tax rate.
It is measured by the average cost of funds (total distortion over total revenue) or the marginal cost of funds (the distortion from the last unit of revenue).
A sales tax discourages buying the taxed goods and an income tax discourages earning taxed income; some people leave work or move into the black economy.
Pigouvian taxes distort on purpose to correct externalities, and so have a negative marginal cost of funds.
'Sin taxes' on alcohol, tobacco and pollution ideally raise the price to what it would be if the external costs were included.

definition.text: Two results linking markets and efficiency: competitive markets reach a Pareto efficient outcome, and any Pareto efficient outcome can be reached by a competitive market from suitable starting endowments.

facts.text: The first theorem needs complete markets, complete information and perfect competition, in which firms and consumers take prices as given.
It is often seen as a formal confirmation of Adam Smith's 'invisible hand'; Kaushik Basu called it the Invisible Hand Theorem.
The market outcome need not be fair: many Pareto efficient allocations exist, including one where one person owns everything.
The second theorem needs stronger conditions, such as convex preferences and convex production sets.
Samuelson, building on Bergson, concluded that any desired ethical goal could be reached through lump-sum taxes or bounties.
Externalities, prominently pollution and climate, often break the theorems' assumptions; in some cases a Pigouvian tax can restore efficiency.
Oskar Lange's 1942 paper set up the now-traditional pair of theorems, one about markets and one about distribution.
The theorems do not generally guarantee that an equilibrium exists or is unique.

title: Greenwald–Stiglitz theorem
article: Fundamental theorems of welfare economics#Greenwald–Stiglitz theorem

definition.text: Bruce Greenwald and Joseph Stiglitz's 1986 result that the welfare theorems fail when markets are incomplete or information is imperfect.

facts.text: With asymmetric information, a competitive equilibrium is generally not even constrained Pareto efficient.
So a government with no better information than private individuals can still find policies that make someone better off and no one worse off.
Example: because of moral hazard, an alcohol tax may be a Pareto improvement by reducing car accidents.

title: Inequity aversion

definition.text: People's preference for fairness and their dislike of unequal outcomes, even when it costs them.

facts.text: In 1999 Fehr and Schmidt modelled people as disliking both being behind others and being ahead of them.
In the ultimatum game, people usually reject low offers, preferring nothing to a small share and in effect paying to punish the proposer.
Willingness to punish those who earn more helps keep cooperation stable, since free riders who earn more get punished.
Capuchin monkeys refused rewards that were handed out unequally in favour of another monkey.

contested_note: Binmore and Shaked attacked Fehr and Schmidt's model for free parameters and unjustified assumptions, and later estimates have contradicted some of its parameters.

definition.text: A tax of a fixed amount that does not depend on the taxpayer's circumstances, so nothing they do can change what they owe.

facts.text: Because people cannot change their behaviour to reduce it, a lump-sum tax creates no deadweight loss.
It is regressive: the lower someone's income, the larger the share of it the tax takes; a per-person version is called a poll tax.
It is rarely used because charging low-income people very large sums relative to income would be politically unacceptable; Switzerland still uses it for some rich foreign residents.
It matters in theory: the second welfare theorem relies on lump-sum transfers to reach a desired efficient outcome.

definition.text: A measure of how much society loses, because taxes distort behaviour, for each extra unit of money the government raises.

facts.text: It is used in the rule for how many public goods to provide, in setting corrective taxes on externalities, and in social cost–benefit analysis.
Pigou (1947) is generally credited with first stating the problem.
In practice it can be calculated from the tax rate and the elasticities of demand and supply.
A common view is that costs of any tax-funded project in a cost–benefit analysis should be scaled up by the marginal cost of funds.

definition.text: Any departure from perfect competition that makes a market settle at a price clearly different from the competitive one, so that people pursuing their own good no longer maximize society's welfare.

facts.text: A distortion can be measured as the gap between a good's market price and its marginal social cost.

Sources include regulation, monopoly, tariffs and import quotas, uncorrected externalities, unequal tax rates, inflation and incomplete information, each of which can cause a net loss of social surplus.
A proportional tax on wages is distorting because it discourages work; a lump-sum tax is not.
Distortions are often responses to market failures, the circumstances that prevent perfect competition.
Revenue from emissions trading could be used to cut distorting taxes, improving the efficiency of climate policy.

definition.text: A breach of the convexity assumptions of basic economics, such as consumers preferring extremes over mixtures or firms with increasing returns to scale.

facts.text: When convexity fails, competitive markets lose many of their good properties: supply and demand may not match, or equilibria may be inefficient.
Example: a zoo that can afford one lion or one eagle wants either whole animal, not half of each, so its preferences are non-convex.
Non-convexities arise with environmental goods and other externalities, as well as in public economics.
The Shapley–Folkman lemma shows that non-convexities still allow approximate equilibria in markets with many consumers.

title: Original position

definition.text: A thought experiment in which people choose the rules of their society from behind a 'veil of ignorance', not knowing what place they will occupy in it.

facts.text: The veil hides each person's ethnicity, social status, gender and idea of a good life, so they must choose impartially; the idea is central to Rawls's 1971 A Theory of Justice.
Rawls argued people would use the maximin rule, judging options by the outcome for the least advantaged.
Vickrey and Harsanyi had earlier used the same thought experiment to show a rational chooser would adopt utilitarianism, maximizing expected well-being.
In a 1987 study, students in a simulated original position preferred maximizing the average with a floor for the worst-off; Rawls's principle was chosen by under 5%.

contested_note: Nozick, Sandel and others dispute Rawls's use of the veil, especially the extreme risk aversion of the maximin rule.

definition.text: The ethical view that judgements of social welfare should give extra weight to benefits for people who are worse off.

facts.text: Like utilitarianism it adds up consequences, but it weights each gain more heavily the worse off the person receiving it is.
Unlike egalitarianism it places no value on equality itself, and unlike maximin it does not look only at the worst-off person.
A main objection is how much extra weight the worse off should get, which risks arbitrariness.
It offers one ethical argument for a high discount rate in climate economics: if future people will be richer, benefits to people today count for more.

definition.text: A situation in which an economy, using today's technology, cannot make more of one good without making less of another.

facts.text: Every point on the production possibility frontier is productively efficient.
An economy is productively inefficient, inside its frontier, when capital or labour sit idle or are put into the wrong industries.
In long-run perfect competition, each good is made at the lowest point of the average total cost curve, where marginal cost equals average total cost.
Productive efficiency says nothing about making the right mix of goods; misapplied, it can produce the wrong basket faster and cheaper.
Monopolies may be productively inefficient through X-inefficiency, though economies of scale can sometimes let them charge less than competitive firms.
Better technology and management can push the production possibility frontier outward.
Data envelopment analysis and stochastic frontier analysis are the most popular ways to estimate it.

definition.text: The finding that the Kaldor compensation test can judge allocation A better than B and also, by the same test, B better than A.

facts.text: It arises when gainers could compensate losers for a change, yet losers could then compensate gainers for switching back.
It is named after the Hungarian-born American economist Tibor Scitovsky, who set out his double criterion in a 1941 paper.
Combining the Kaldor and Hicks tests removes this flaw, but the combined criterion may still not be transitive.

definition.text: The branch of welfare economics that studies how individual preferences can be combined into good collective decisions.

facts.text: It is normative, asking how a society should decide, unlike political science, which describes how societies actually decide.
Constitutions, parliamentary voting procedures and electoral systems are real-world social choice rules, so the field is sometimes called voting theory.
It began with the Marquis de Condorcet; Kenneth Arrow's book Social Choice and Individual Values opened its modern era.
Two classic rules are the utilitarian rule, which maximizes the sum of utilities, and the egalitarian or Rawlsian rule, which maximizes the smallest utility.
Gibbard's theorem shows that with three or more outcomes no voting rule can always make honest voting the best strategy.
In 1970 Amartya Sen's Collective Choice and Social Welfare brought comparisons between people and the idea of capability into the field.
Later work extended social choice to fair division, legal compensation and natural resources, among other topics.

definition.text: The finding that majority voting over three or more options can go round in a circle: A beats B, B beats C, yet C beats A.

facts.text: It shows democracy cannot simply equal majority rule, which becomes self-contradictory with three or more options.
With only two options, May's theorem shows simple majority is the best rule.
A review of 37 studies covering 265 real elections found 25 cases of the paradox, a likelihood of 9.4%.

title: Interpersonal utility comparison

definition.text: The disputed question of whether one person's gain or loss in well-being can be measured and weighed against another's.

facts.text: Following Bentham, utilitarians argue utilities can be compared and added up into a total for society to maximize.
Diminishing marginal utility has been used to justify transfers from rich to poor, since the poor gain more from an extra unit of income.
Lionel Robbins argued such comparisons are unscientific and cannot be tested.
Harsanyi and Sen reply that at least partial comparisons are possible, so social choice should proceed on that basis.

contested_note: Robbins and his followers deny that utility can be compared across people, while Harsanyi and Sen argue partial comparison is possible.

definition.text: An imaginary decision-maker used in economic models who chooses everyone's allocations to maximize a social welfare function.

facts.text: The planner's problem is a constrained optimization; solving it for every set of weights on people yields all Pareto efficient allocations.
Solving it would require knowing everyone's preferences and every resource limit, so economists ask whether decentralized markets can reach the same outcomes; the welfare theorems answer this.
Ramsey first framed his growth model as a social planner maximizing total consumption across generations.

definition.text: The gap a tax opens between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive for a good.

facts.text: With a tax, consumers pay more, suppliers receive less, and the quantity traded falls; the price gap equals the per-unit tax.
The wedge-shaped area on a supply-and-demand diagram equals the deadweight loss of the tax, one half times the tax times the fall in quantity.
A monopoly pricing above marginal cost drives a similar wedge between what consumers pay and what it costs to supply.

title: Tax incidence

definition.text: Who actually bears the cost of a tax, which may differ from who legally hands the money to the government.

facts.text: Statutory incidence falls on whoever pays the government; economic incidence falls on whoever really bears the cost, and the first does not determine the second.
Economic incidence depends entirely on the elasticities of supply and demand: the side less able to adjust bears more.
Smokers bear most of a tobacco tax because their demand barely responds to price, while owners of beachfront hotels bear most of a hotel tax because supply cannot change.
In the long run supply and demand become more elastic, so the split of the burden can shift.

contested_note: Public finance economists disagree greatly on how far market forces shift the burden of particular taxes.

definition.text: The result that when one condition for an ideal economy cannot be met, the best remaining option may require moving other conditions away from their ideal values too.

facts.text: Richard Lipsey and Kelvin Lancaster showed this in 1956.
If one market distortion cannot be removed, adding another distortion in a linked market may partly offset it and raise efficiency.
Fixing a market failure in one sector while an uncorrectable failure remains in a related sector can lower overall efficiency.
A common error, the 'fallacy of exhaustive effort', assumes meeting as many remaining ideal conditions as possible gives the second-best result.
Example: liberalising trade while ignoring an environmental externality, because 'free trade is good', can leave welfare lower than doing nothing.
When the externality itself cannot be taxed, taxing a related product can be the second-best Pigouvian solution.

definition.text: A family of ethical theories holding that the right action is the one that produces the most happiness and well-being for everyone affected.

facts.text: Jeremy Bentham founded it; his successor John Stuart Mill reshaped it and popularized the word 'utilitarianism'.
Bentham proposed measuring pleasures and pains by their intensity, duration, certainty and nearness, a method called the hedonic calculus.
Mill rejected a purely quantitative measure, arguing some kinds of pleasure are more valuable than others.
Its ideas have been applied to welfare economics, justice, global poverty, the ethics of raising animals for food and existential risks.
In social choice, the utilitarian rule picks the option that maximizes the sum of everyone's utilities.
Wealth maximization, an offshoot tied to Kaldor–Hicks efficiency, allows changes that raise total surplus even if some lose, as long as winners could compensate losers.
Critics object that well-being cannot be measured or compared, and Rawls argued it ignores the distinction between persons.
Utilitarian thinking underlies one of the two main approaches to animal ethics, most associated with Peter Singer.

definition.text: A curve showing the most utility one person can have for each level of utility the others have, given society's resources; the welfare counterpart of the production possibility frontier.

facts.text: Every point on the frontier is Pareto efficient; points inside it are not, and points beyond it cannot be reached.
Its slope shows how much one person's utility must fall for another's to rise.
It is derived from the contract curve, re-drawn in terms of utilities instead of goods.
Choosing among its points needs a social welfare function; the best is where it touches society's highest indifference curve, called the 'point of bliss'.
